# PowerShell Launched With an Encoded Command

`win_proc_encoded_powershell` · Sigma id `d46fb37c-e191-40be-afc1-00a1815513e7` · status `experimental` · level `medium`

## Goal

Catch PowerShell being run with a base64-encoded command, so the real script is hidden from anyone reading the command line. It's a staple of malicious Office macros, phishing loaders, and post-exploitation frameworks.

## ATT&CK

- [T1059.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/) PowerShell
- Tactic: Execution (TA0002)

Checked against pinned ATT&CK v20.1 by `ringtail validate`.

## Log source

product: `windows`, category: `process_creation`

## Detection logic

Fires when a process is PowerShell (Windows PowerShell or PowerShell 7, matched by path or by the original file name in the PE header, which catches renamed copies) and its command line uses -EncodedCommand or any abbreviation PowerShell accepts for it (-e, -en, -enc, -enco..., -ec). Slashes and look-alike dashes count too.

Exact logic, generated from the rule:

- **selection_img**: any one of
  - `Image` ends with any of `'\powershell.exe'`, `'\pwsh.exe'`
  - `OriginalFileName` is any of `'PowerShell.EXE'`, `'pwsh.dll'`
- **selection_enc**: `CommandLine` contains any of `' -e '`, `' -en '`, `' -enc '`, `' -enco'`, `' -ec '` (also matches `/` and Unicode dash look-alikes in place of `-`)
- **Condition**: `all of selection_*`

## Known false positives

- Management and deployment tools (SCCM, Intune, some RMM agents) that legitimately pass encoded commands
- Admin scripts that build PowerShell command lines with -EncodedCommand to avoid quoting issues

## Triage steps

1. Decode the payload. It's base64 of UTF-16LE text. In PowerShell: `[Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetString([Convert]::FromBase64String('<b64>'))`, or CyberChef "From Base64" then "Decode text (UTF-16LE)". Do this on an analysis box, never by running the command.
2. Check the parent process. Office apps, browsers, `wscript.exe`, `mshta.exe`, or `explorer.exe` from a user session are high suspicion. Management agents (`CcmExec.exe`, `IntuneManagementExtension.exe`, a known RMM agent) are usually benign; confirm against your baseline.
3. Look at what the decoded script does: downloads (`DownloadString`, `Invoke-WebRequest`, `Net.WebClient`), `IEX`, AMSI or Defender tampering, credential access. If PowerShell Script Block Logging is on, event 4104 shows the decoded content too.
4. If `Image` isn't `powershell.exe` or `pwsh.exe` but `OriginalFileName` is, someone renamed PowerShell to blend in. Escalate.
5. Pull follow-on activity from the same process and host: network connections (Sysmon 3), child processes, file writes, and logons around that time. Check whether the user normally runs admin scripts.
6. If it's malicious: isolate the host, preserve evidence, and hunt the decoded indicators (URLs, hashes, file names) across the rest of the fleet.

## Test results

**PASS**: 4/4 true-positive samples matched, 3/3 false-positive samples correctly ignored.

| Sample | Should fire | Fired | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classic short flag: powershell.exe -enc &lt;base64&gt;. Decodes to: Write-Output 'ringtail test' | yes | yes | pass |
| Full flag name in caps, launched from Word. Sigma matching is case-insensitive. Decodes to a download cradle aimed at example.invalid. | yes | yes | pass |
| PowerShell 7 with the -ec alias. | yes | yes | pass |
| Renamed binary: Image is not powershell.exe, but OriginalFileName (from the PE header) still is. | yes | yes | pass |
| Routine admin PowerShell running a script file. No encoding. | no | no | pass |
| Interactive admin command. -ExecutionPolicy starts with -e but is not an encoding flag. | no | no | pass |
| Not PowerShell: openssl uses -e for encrypt. Proves the image selection is required. | no | no | pass |
